reconcile.connective: Commentators distinguish God as impartial judge — who weighs no man's outward status — from God as sovereign benefactor, who freely accepted Abel's faith over Cain's.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, lists this exact pairing — God's respect for Abel over Cain in Genesis 4 against the stack of verses (Deut 10:17; Acts 10:34; Rom 2:11; etc.) declaring God no respecter of persons — as a standing contradiction.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible ("Does God respect anyone?")
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Does God respect anyone?" (SAB Books, 2013), skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/respect.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: that God is no respecter of persons—Not, "I see there is no capricious favoritism with God," for Peter would never imagine such a thing; but (as the next clause shows), "I see that God has respect only to personal character and state in the acceptance of men, national and ecclesiastical distinctions being of no account."
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Defines 'no respecter of persons' as the absence of favoritism toward outward national/ecclesiastical status, not the absence of all preference — God still has respect to personal character, which is exactly the Abel-vs-Cain ground.

excerpts.excerpt_text: God, as a benefactor, gives favours arbitrarily and by sovereignty (Deu 7:7, Deu 7:8; Deu 9:5, Deu 9:6; Mat 20:10); but he does not, as a judge, so give sentence; but in every nation, and under ever denomination, he that fears God and works righteousness is accepted of him, Act 10:35.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Supplies the explicit benefactor/judge distinction that reconciles the two poles: God's sovereign bestowal of favour (Abel) is a different act from his impartial judicial sentence ('no respecter of persons').

excerpts.excerpt_text: A judge, as such, is to regard no man's person, but to proceed in matters before him, according to the rules of law and justice; should he do otherwise, he would be chargeable with being a respecter of persons; but then he may bestow alms on what objects he pleases; and forgive one man who is personally indebted to him, and not another, without any such imputation. … though God, as a Judge, respects no man's person; yet in matters of grace he distinguishes one person from another, as it is plain he does by the bounties of his Providence.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly applies the judicial-impartiality / sovereign-grace distinction to the contradiction: God-as-judge respects no person, yet in matters of grace (the Abel case) he freely distinguishes — the ellipsis joins the principle to its stated application without altering sense.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Acts 10:34
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact tension at Acts 10:34, distinguishing God as sovereign benefactor (who gives favours 'arbitrarily and by sovereignty') from God as impartial judge, and ties the principle back to Genesis 4:7.
